nameStory: The 'purple coneflower' gets its name from its distinctive droopy purple petals that surround a prominent cone-shaped center. The cone feels prickly to the touch, which inspired its scientific name Echinacea - from the Greek word 'echinos' meaning hedgehog or sea urchin. Some folks also call it the hedgehog coneflower for this same spiky characteristic!
description: Purple coneflower is a cheerful perennial wildflower that stands 2-4 feet tall with distinctive daisy-like blooms. The flowers feature drooping purple-pink petals (technically called ray petals) that curve backward from a prominent orange-brown spiky center cone. The sturdy stems hold the flowers well above the foliage, making them easy to spot in meadows and gardens. This native beauty blooms from mid-summer into fall, attracting butterflies and goldfinches to its nectar and seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large daisy-like blooms with 8-21 drooping purple-pink petals that curve backward from a prominent spiky orange-brown center cone that feels rough and prickly to gentle touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rough-textured, sandpaper-like leaves that are lance-shaped with prominent veins and toothed edges, arranged alternately on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 2-4 feet tall with sturdy, hairy stems that hold flowers well above the foliage

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark brown to black seeds develop in the spiky cone center, often persisting into winter and attracting goldfinches

habitat: In New England, purple coneflower thrives in sunny, well-drained locations including meadows, prairie restorations, roadsides, and open woodland edges. While native to areas further west and south, it has naturalized in parts of our region and is widely planted in gardens and wildflower plantings. Look for it in areas with full sun to light shade, often growing alongside other native wildflowers like black-eyed Susan and wild bergamot.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of rough, lance-shaped leaves close to the ground. Young plants focus energy on establishing strong root systems before sending up flower stalks.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from July through August, with distinctive purple flowers on tall stems attracting butterflies, bees, and other pollinators throughout the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into September, then seed heads develop and mature. The spiky brown cones become magnets for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.
seasonality.winter: Sturdy dried stems and persistent seed heads remain standing, providing food for birds and winter interest. The dried cones retain their characteristic spiky texture even when covered with snow.

funFact: The spiky center cone contains a natural compound that makes your tongue tingle and go slightly numb when you chew it - indigenous peoples traditionally used this 'tingle test' to identify genuine Echinacea plants for medicinal purposes!
confusionNotes: Purple coneflower is sometimes confused with wild bergamot or other purple wildflowers, but the distinctive backward-curving petals and prominent spiky cone center make it unmistakable. Remember: if the petals droop down like a sad daisy around a prickly orange cone, you've found your purple coneflower!
contextualKnowledge: This is the same Echinacea that's sold as an herbal supplement in health stores, though the commercial products are usually made from the roots rather than the flowers. Many people don't realize that the popular immune-boosting herb comes from this beautiful native wildflower that's perfectly at home in New England gardens.
compareHints: Purple coneflower differs from its relative pale purple coneflower by having wider, more overlapping petals that are deeper purple-pink in color. Pale purple coneflower has narrower, more separated petals that are lighter in color and often appear more sparse around the central cone. Purple coneflower is also more commonly found and better adapted to New England conditions than its paler cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative purple coneflower, pale purple coneflower has much more drooping, narrower petals and a lighter color.
